papers.title: The Counterfeit Conundrum: Can Code Language Models Grasp the Nuances of Their Incorrect Generations?
papers.abstract: Code language models often produce incorrect programs, including subtle “counterfeit” samples that pass weak checks. This paper studies whether models can understand such samples via correctness checking, execution prediction, and repair. Across HumanEval, LeetCode, and ODEX, most models struggle to distinguish counterfeit from correct programs, frequently predict counterfeit execution as if the code were correct, and often repair counterfeits less successfully than simple resampling. The paper further finds that counterfeit difficulty is only weakly related to problem difficulty, that models do not treat their own counterfeits differently from others’, and that both strong and weak models can generate similarly challenging counterfeits. The authors conclude that self-verification and self-repair should be used with caution when no external feedback is available.

papers.title: The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: Sketching is a localized program synthesis approach in which programmers write partial programs that capture the high-level structure of a solution while leaving low-level details unspecified. A synthesis engine fills in the missing code using a specification such as a reference implementation or test harnesses. The paper presents the Sketch language and synthesizer, explains techniques that make synthesis from sketches tractable, and illustrates the approach with examples including linked-list reversal and a concurrent barrier. It also briefly discusses open problems in programmer-guided synthesis.

papers.title: Smoothing a Program Soundly and Robustly
papers.abstract: The paper studies foundations of smooth interpretation, a program approximation technique based on Gaussian convolution of program semantics. It defines three correctness properties for approximate smooth interpreters: soundness, robustness, and β-robustness. Soundness means the approximation encloses the exact smoothed semantics; robustness requires the computed function to have derivatives of all orders with bounded partial derivatives; β-robustness bounds sensitivity to the smoothing parameter. The authors present an approximate smooth interpreter that combines abstract interpretation with symbolic convolution of interval-guarded linear programs, then prove it satisfies these properties under a weak condition on β.

papers.title: Euler: A System for Numerical Optimization of Programs
papers.abstract: We give a tutorial introduction to Euler, a system for solving difficult optimization problems involving programs. Euler treats a program as an optimization target, using smooth interpretation to replace discontinuous program behavior with smooth approximations. The paper illustrates the approach with a parallel-parking controller synthesis example, explains how Euler compiles sketches into executables, and describes its iterative smoothing and optimization loop. Results show that smoothing improves numerical search compared with running Nelder-Mead directly on the original program.

papers.title: Adaptive Concretization for Parallel Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: Program synthesis tools often use either symbolic search or explicit search. This paper presents adaptive concretization, a hybrid synthesis algorithm that partially concretizes a randomly chosen subset of unknowns, with emphasis on highly influential unknowns. The method estimates influential holes using a local graph-based heuristic, then searches online for an effective degree of concretization using exponential climbing, binary search, and a statistical comparison test. The approach is designed to parallelize naturally across many trials. Implemented in Sketch, adaptive concretization was evaluated on 26 benchmarks from multiple synthesis domains, where it often outperformed pure symbolic search and scaled reasonably on 1, 4, and 32 cores.

papers.abstract: Spt is a storyboard programming tool for synthesizing low-level data-structure manipulations from abstract and concrete input-output examples, implementation skeletons, and intermediate state descriptions. papers.title: StatusQuo: Making Familiar Abstractions Perform Using Program Analysis
papers.abstract: StatusQuo is a system for database-backed web applications that uses program analysis and synthesis to move functionality between application and database layers. It can extract SQL from imperative Java code using QBS, and partition programs across application and database servers using dynamic workload-aware code placement. The paper presents prototype results on real-world Java/Hibernate benchmarks and TPC-C/TPC-W workloads, showing that automatic transformation and adaptive partitioning can approach manually optimized implementations while reducing developer burden.

papers.title: Using Program Synthesis for Social Recommendations
papers.abstract: This paper presents a hybrid approach for personalized social recommendations in the LifeJoin setting. It combines program synthesis with machine learning to learn user preferences from liked and disliked events, while producing decomposable, human-understandable models that can be pushed to mobile devices for data acquisition and filtering. The method uses Sketch to synthesize candidate boolean interest functions, extracts predicates from them, and trains an SVM over those predicates; it also uses synthesis to generate decomposable explanations from SVM support vectors. Experiments on synthetic LifeJoin-style data show improved training time, better active learning behavior, and higher classification accuracy than several standard baselines, especially under noise and in large domains.

papers.title: JoinABLe: Learning Bottom-up Assembly of Parametric CAD Joints
papers.abstract: JoinABLe is a learning-based method for assembling pairs of CAD parts by predicting parametric joints from weak supervision in standard parametric CAD files. It uses B-Rep graph representations, a joint-axis prediction network, and a neurally guided joint-pose search to recover editable joints without object class labels or human guidance. The paper introduces the Fusion 360 Gallery assembly dataset with assembly, joint, contact, and hole metadata. Experiments show JoinABLe outperforms several point-cloud and B-Rep baselines, approaching human CAD expert performance on joint-axis prediction.

papers.title: LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
papers.abstract: We study LINC, a neurosymbolic approach to logical reasoning that uses a language model as a semantic parser from natural language to first-order logic, then delegates deduction to an external theorem prover, with majority voting over multiple samples. Evaluated on FOLIO and a balanced subset of ProofWriter, LINC improves performance over naïve prompting, scratchpad, and chain-of-thought baselines across nearly all conditions. The gains are especially large for smaller or open-source models and on ProofWriter, where LINC reaches near-ceiling accuracy for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Error analysis shows that LINC and chain-of-thought fail in different ways: LINC is mostly limited by semantic parsing losses and syntax errors, while chain-of-thought more often makes incorrect or incomplete deductions. The results suggest that combining language models with symbolic provers can substantially improve reliable logical reasoning.

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs, the Missing Link in Agentic AI-based Formal Verification
papers.abstract: Recent advances in LLMs enable SystemVerilog Assertion synthesis from natural-language specifications, but ambiguity, missing design details, and weak specification-to-RTL grounding cause semantic mismatches and syntax failures. This paper proposes a verification-centric knowledge graph built from structured intermediate representations of specifications, RTL, and formal-tool feedback (syntax diagnostics, counterexamples, and coverage reports). A multi-agent workflow queries and updates the KG to generate and refine SVAs through syntax repair, CEX-guided correction, and coverage-directed augmentation. Evaluation on seven benchmark designs shows improved grounding and compilable SVAs with low syntax-repair overhead, with formal coverage ranging from 78.5% to 99.4%. Remaining limitations are most evident in complex temporal and arithmetic reasoning.

papers.title: Verifiably Safe Exploration for End-to-End Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: This paper proposes Verifiably Safe Reinforcement Learning (VSRL) for safe exploration with visual inputs. The method combines pretrained object detection with formally verified safety monitors synthesized from differential dynamic logic models of the safety-relevant dynamics. During reinforcement learning, unsafe actions are replaced by sampled safe actions, enabling end-to-end policies to learn from images while preserving hard safety constraints. The paper proves that the wrapper preserves safety along trajectories and that, when applied to a convergent RL algorithm, it converges to the reward-optimal safe policy. Experiments on XO, adaptive cruise control, goal-finding, and pointmesses environments show zero safety violations during training and competitive reward performance, including in reward-misaligned settings that expose reward hacking.

papers.title: Synthesizing Programmatic Policies that Inductively Generalize
papers.abstract: We propose an algorithm for learning programmatic state machine policies for continuous control tasks that generalize to novel environments requiring arbitrary repetitions. The method, called adaptive teaching, alternates between a teacher that optimizes loop-free trajectories and a student that learns a structured state-machine policy by imitation. The teacher is regularized to match the student’s structure, and the student is trained with an EM-style procedure over latent mode assignments. Experiments on several reinforcement learning benchmarks show that the learned policies generalize better than standard neural network policies and remain interpretable.

papers.title: LIVECODEBENCH: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
papers.abstract: LIVECODEBENCH is a live, contamination-free benchmark for evaluating large language models on code. It curates competition problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces with release dates, allowing time-segmented evaluation to reduce contamination and detect overfitting. Beyond code generation, it measures self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction to assess broader programming capabilities relevant to agents. The benchmark emphasizes curated problems, robust test-based evaluation, and difficulty-based filtering. The paper reports results for more than 50 models and shows contamination effects, differences across scenarios, and evidence that HumanEval can be saturated and overfit relative to LIVECODEBENCH.

papers.title: VLMaterial: Procedural Material Generation with Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: We present VLMaterial, a single-image procedural material generation method that fine-tunes a large vision-language model to predict Blender procedural materials in Python code. By transpiling material node graphs into programs, the model can generate editable materials directly from images. To address data scarcity, we introduce an open-source Blender procedural material dataset and a two-stage augmentation strategy: program-structure evolution using a pre-trained LLM and node-parameter augmentation. A fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT model outperforms prior methods on synthetic and real images, and a gradient-free MCMC post-optimization further refines material parameters for better perceptual matching.

papers.title: Representing partial programs with blended abstract semantics
papers.abstract: The paper introduces blended abstract semantics, a hybrid representation for partially written programs in program synthesis. It combines concrete execution on completed subexpressions with learned neural approximate semantics for holes and other unexecuted parts, inspired by abstract interpretation. The representation is used to train search policies and value functions for goal-conditioned synthesis. Experiments on tower construction, list processing with higher-order functions, and string editing show that the method outperforms neural baselines and can handle language constructs that are difficult for execution-guided synthesis.

papers.title: Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
papers.abstract: The paper studies whether self-repair improves code generation when the cost of feedback and repair is included. Using CodeLlama-13b-instruct, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS, the authors compare self-repair against i.i.d. sampling under equal budgets. They find self-repair is often only modestly helpful, can underperform baselines at smaller budgets, and benefits more from spending budget on diverse initial samples than on many repairs. They also show that stronger feedback models substantially improve repair, and that human feedback can outperform model-only self-repair even for GPT-4.

papers.title: A large-scale benchmark for few-shot program induction and synthesis
papers.abstract: The paper introduces PROGRES (Programs from Real Executed Subproblems), a large-scale benchmark for few-shot program induction and synthesis built from real CodeForces C++ programs and their unit tests. By extracting subprograms from executing full programs and propagating human-designed tests to intermediate code segments, the authors construct over 200,000 tasks with input-output examples, text context, type signatures, and code. They analyze dataset properties, equivalence checking, slicing, and a C++ interpreter/emulator pipeline, then evaluate transformer-based baselines for both program induction and program synthesis. Results show that synthesis generally outperforms direct induction when programs are sliced, pretrained models help, and adding text context improves performance. The benchmark is intended to support research in few-shot learning, neural program synthesis, and code understanding.

papers.title: Neurosymbolic World Models for Sequential Decision Making
papers.abstract: We present Structured World Modeling for Policy Optimization (SWMPO), an unsupervised neurosymbolic framework that learns finite-state-machine world models from low-level continuous observations. SWMPO first learns reusable neural primitives for distinct environment modes, then synthesizes an environment-specific FSM by clustering latent mode vectors, pruning spurious transitions, and learning transition predicates. The resulting structured world model is used for model-based reinforcement learning and policy optimization from offline and limited online data. Experiments on simulated navigation and locomotion tasks show that SWMPO improves latent mode tracking over HMM, SLDS, and rSLDS baselines and can outperform model-free and monolithic model-based RL on Point Mass.

papers.title: Future Research and Challenges Remain Towards AI for Software Engineering
papers.abstract: AI for software engineering has made remarkable progress, but major challenges remain before full automation is practical. This position paper proposes a taxonomy of SWE tasks using scope, logical complexity, and human intervention, covering generation, transformation, testing, analysis, maintenance, scaffolding, and formal verification. It then identifies four cross-cutting challenges: data, scale, interaction, and measurement. Finally, it outlines future directions including community data collection, richer program annotations, neurosymbolic methods, stronger tool integration, and improved human supervision to advance AI-driven software engineering.

papers.title: CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
papers.abstract: We present CRUXEval, a benchmark of 800 short Python functions paired with input-output examples for two tasks: output prediction and input prediction. Candidates are generated with Code Llama 34B and filtered for short, low-computation, deterministic programs. Evaluations on 20 code models show that many strong HumanEval models do not improve much on CRUXEval, while GPT-4 performs best but still fails on some simple programs. The paper also analyzes correlations with HumanEval, compares input vs. output prediction, studies chain-of-thought prompting and fine-tuning, and highlights common failure modes in code execution and reasoning.

papers.title: When Do Skills Help Reinforcement Learning? A Theoretical Analysis of Temporal Abstractions
papers.abstract: Skills are temporal abstractions meant to improve reinforcement learning via hierarchical RL. This paper gives a theoretical and empirical characterization of when deterministic skills help in deterministic sparse-reward environments with finite action spaces. The authors define p-learning difficulty and p-exploration difficulty, relate them to sample complexity, and introduce incompressibility measures for solution trajectories. They prove lower bounds showing that less compressible environments benefit less from skills, that skills tend to help exploration more than learning from experience, and that unexpressive skills such as macroactions can sometimes worsen performance. Experiments on CliffWalking, CompILE2, 8Puzzle, and RubiksCube222 support these results and connect the theory to skill-discovery objectives.

papers.title: Learning to Infer Program Sketches
papers.abstract: We present SKETCHADAPT, a neuro-symbolic program synthesis system that learns to dynamically balance neural pattern recognition and symbolic search. The model generates program sketches from specifications such as input-output examples or natural language, then fills sketch holes with enumerative synthesis. A self-supervised training objective learns how detailed sketches should be for different tasks and time budgets. Experiments on list processing, string transformation, and the AlgoLisp description-to-code dataset show improved data efficiency and strong generalization over generator-only and synthesizer-only baselines.

papers.title: Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: Program synthesis via constraint solving can become slow when many input-output examples are encoded. This paper proposes an iterative method to select a small, representative subset of examples using a neural network that estimates how likely unchosen examples are given the chosen subset. The least probable example is added greedily until the remaining examples are sufficiently anticipated. The selected subset is then used to seed CEGIS, combining representative-example discovery with counterexample-guided synthesis. Experiments on ordering synthesis, DFA synthesis, and programmatic drawing show improved synthesis time and stability over baselines.

papers.title: Predicate Exchange: Inference with Declarative Knowledge
papers.abstract: We present predicate exchange, a likelihood-free inference method for conditioning probabilistic models on broad declarative predicates. The method relaxes hard predicates into soft predicates over a continuous Boolean algebra, then uses a replica-exchange MCMC scheme to sample from the true posterior or an approximation when predicates are measure-zero. The paper formalizes predicate relaxation, soft logical primitives, and nonstandard execution for probabilistic programs, and demonstrates the approach on inverse rendering and glucose forecasting.

papers.title: A Language for Counterfactual Generative Models
papers.abstract: We present OMEGAC, a probabilistic programming language with support for counterfactual inference. The language introduces a do-like operator for interventions, defines formal semantics, and implements counterfactual reasoning by combining intervention and conditioning. OMEGAC uses lazy evaluation and retroactive updating to preserve dependencies under intervention. The paper demonstrates the language on simulation-based examples including a car-crash model, glucose modeling, counterfactual planning, and but-for causality in occlusion, and argues that do is not expressible as syntactic sugar.

papers.title: Bench-Push: Benchmarking Pushing-based Navigation and Manipulation Tasks for Mobile Robots
papers.abstract: Mobile robots in cluttered environments often must interact with movable objects rather than avoid all contacts. This paper presents Bench-Push, a unified benchmark for pushing-based mobile robot navigation and manipulation tasks. It includes configurable 2D and 3D simulated environments for maze navigation, ship navigation in ice, box delivery, and area clearing; novel metrics for efficiency, interaction effort, and partial completion; and baseline implementations using reinforcement learning and task-specific planners. The paper also reports sim-to-real experiments on a TurtleBot3 testbed, showing that behaviors and performance trends transfer reasonably from simulation to hardware.

papers.title: MANTRA: Synthesizing SMT-Validated Compliance Benchmarks for Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: MANTRA is a framework for automatically synthesizing machine-checkable compliance benchmarks for tool-using LLM agents from natural-language procedural manuals and tool schemas. It builds scenarios by sampling document regions, generates trace-level compliance checks, and independently creates a symbolic world model. The two artifacts are cross-validated with SMT solving, and inconsistencies are repaired through a structured loop with human intervention only as fallback. The paper reports a new benchmark suite with 285 tasks across 6 domains, spanning manuals of 50+ pages, and shows that the resulting checks are richer and more deterministic than existing benchmarks. MANTRA is also used to analyze agent failure modes and debug compliance violations.

papers.title: The Three Pillars of Machine Programming
papers.abstract: This position paper presents a vision for machine programming organized around three pillars: intention, invention, and adaptation. Intention addresses richer human-to-computer interaction for expressing goals. Invention concerns discovering or refining algorithms and core building blocks using machine learning and synthesis. Adaptation focuses on automatically evolving software for new hardware, bugs, vulnerabilities, and changing workloads. The paper argues that recent advances in machine learning, program analysis, data availability, and heterogeneous computing make machine programming increasingly feasible, and it discusses the interplay among the three pillars and the central role of data.

papers.title: Verifiable Reinforcement Learning via Policy Extraction
papers.abstract: The paper proposes verifying reinforcement-learning policies by extracting decision tree policies from deep neural network oracles. It introduces VIPER, an imitation-learning and model-compression based algorithm that uses the oracle’s Q-function to train smaller, more verifiable decision trees than DAGGER. The method is evaluated on Atari Pong, a toy Pong game, cart-pole, and half-cheetah. The paper also shows how to verify properties such as robustness, correctness, and stability of the extracted policies using SMT, Z3, and sum-of-squares techniques. The extracted trees match the original DNN policies’ performance in the studied tasks, while enabling substantially more efficient verification.

papers.title: Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction
papers.abstract: The paper presents EC2, a program induction algorithm that learns a domain-specific language (DSL) while jointly training a neural recognition model to guide search. EC2 alternates between exploring programs, compressing them into reusable library fragments, and compiling a neural model to amortize search. It is applied to list processing, text editing, and symbolic regression, where it discovers new subroutines and improves program synthesis performance over fixed-DSL baselines. The work frames this as approximate Bayesian inference over DSLs and programs, using fragment-based DSL induction and neural posterior approximation.

papers.title: Learning to Infer Graphics Programs from Hand-Drawn Images
papers.abstract: We introduce a model that converts simple hand drawings into graphics programs written in a subset of LaTeX. The approach combines deep learning and program synthesis in two stages: a convolutional network infers drawing primitives (a spec) from an image, and a synthesis system recovers a high-level graphics program from that spec. The resulting programs can include variable bindings, loops, reflections, and conditionals, enabling error correction and extrapolation of drawings. The paper reports experiments on synthetic diagrams and real hand-drawn figures, and introduces learned search policies to make program synthesis practical.

papers.title: Unsupervised Learning by Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: We introduce an unsupervised learning algorithm that combines probabilistic modeling with solver-based techniques for program synthesis. papers.title: Sampling for Bayesian Program Learning
papers.abstract: We introduce program sampling for Bayesian program learning: drawing programs from posterior distributions conditioned on examples or specifications. The method combines constraint-based program synthesis with random XOR-parity constraints to approximately sample from high-tilt program spaces, then corrects the proposal with rejection sampling. The paper gives theoretical guarantees on approximation quality and evaluates the approach on 22 program induction problems in text editing and list manipulation, showing practical sampling performance and useful posterior predictive uncertainty.

papers.title: MeMo: Meaningful, Modular Controllers via Noise Injection
papers.abstract: Robots are often built from standardized assemblies, but controllers are typically retrained from scratch for each morphology. This paper presents MeMo, a framework that learns meaningful modular controllers from a single robot and expert controller, then reuses assembly-specific modules to accelerate transfer to new morphologies and tasks. MeMo introduces a modularity objective that encourages a narrow, robust interface between a boss controller and worker modules, optimized jointly with behavior cloning through Gaussian noise injection. Experiments in locomotion and grasping show improved training efficiency over graph neural network and Transformer baselines for structure transfer and task transfer. Ablations indicate that noise injection is the key component enabling better modular responsibility division and lower-dimensional actuator representations.

papers.title: Program Synthesis Guided Reinforcement Learning for Partially Observed Environments
papers.abstract: We propose model predictive program synthesis (MPPS), which automatically synthesizes guiding programs for program-guided reinforcement learning in partially observed environments. MPPS learns a conditional generative model of the unobserved world, samples possible completions, and uses MaxSAT-based synthesis to find a program that is robust to uncertainty. The resulting agent alternates between hallucinating hidden state, synthesizing a high-level program, and executing learned options. Experiments on 2D-craft, box-world, and a MuJoCo ant-craft transfer setting show that MPPS substantially outperforms non-program-guided baselines and approaches the performance of oracle handcrafted programs.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Network Judgments via Minimal, Stable, and Symbolic Corrections
papers.abstract: We present an algorithm that generates minimal, stable, and symbolic corrections for an input to a ReLU neural network so that the network’s output changes to a desired class. The method solves a series of linear constraint satisfaction problems, growing verified linear regions around an initial concrete correction and then inferring a simple convex symbolic correction such as a simplex or box. The approach is evaluated on three judgment tasks: mortgage underwriting, first-order theorem solving performance prediction, and drawing tutoring. Experiments show that the method often finds small, actionable corrections and scales to a multiclass extension with similar runtime.

papers.title: sk_p: a neural program corrector for MOOCs
papers.abstract: We present a technique for automatic program correction in MOOCs that fixes syntactic and semantic errors without manual, problem-specific strategies. Given an incorrect student program, the system generates candidate corrections from a learned distribution and checks them against a test suite. It treats program statements syntactically, using a seq2seq-style neural model to predict missing statements from local context. The method corrects 29% of incorrect submissions and outperforms a prior approach that relies on manual correction models.

papers.title: From Equations to Algorithms and Data: Transforming Microwave Engineering and Education with Machine Learning
papers.abstract: This paper argues for a pedagogical shift in microwave and RFIC education from topology-driven analytical design toward machine-learning- and data-driven electromagnetic synthesis. It proposes integrating inverse design, surrogate modeling, reinforcement learning, Bayesian optimization, and multi-objective optimization into microwave curricula for components such as power dividers, couplers, and baluns. The framework preserves classical electromagnetic intuition while enabling specification-driven exploration of larger design spaces, including millimeter-wave and terahertz regimes. The paper also outlines course material, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and implementation strategies, emphasizing project-based learning, physics-based validation, and industry-relevant tools.

papers.title: Faceted Execution of Policy-Agnostic Programs
papers.abstract: The paper extends Jeeves, a policy-agnostic programming language for confidentiality, with faceted execution. Sensitive values are represented explicitly as facets, allowing the runtime to propagate multiple views of data, improve expressiveness, and reason about runtime behavior. The authors define a dynamic semantics for the core language λjeeves, prove termination-insensitive non-interference and policy compliance, and describe a Scala implementation using Z3. A conference-management case study demonstrates practical use of the system.

papers.title: Reduced-Order Modeling of Parameterized Visco-Plastic Shallow Flows
papers.abstract: We propose a non-intrusive reduced-order modeling framework for parametrized visco-plastic free-surface flows governed by a shallow-water formulation of Herschel–Bulkley fluids. The method uses a tensor-based low-rank representation obtained by higher-order singular value decomposition of snapshot data over a structured parameter grid. The resulting tensorial reduced-order model reconstructs solution trajectories directly from the compressed representation, avoiding time integration of a reduced dynamical system. Numerical experiments show accurate recovery of flow fronts, plug and shear regions, and near-stopping dynamics, with substantial speedups over full-order simulations.

papers.title: Stencil-Lifting: Hierarchical Recursive Lifting System for Extracting Summary of Stencil Kernel in Legacy Codes
papers.abstract: Stencil-Lifting is a system for translating legacy Fortran stencil kernels into semantically equivalent Halide DSL code. It introduces hierarchical recursive lifting based on invariant subgraphs to summarize nested loops without search-based synthesis. The method derives predicate-based vertex summaries, uses recursive propagation across loop levels, and proves termination and completeness. Evaluations on benchmark suites and real-world applications show large speedups over STNG and Dexter while preserving semantic equivalence.

papers.title: Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types
papers.abstract: We present a method for synthesizing recursive functions that provably satisfy specifications written as polymorphic refinement types. The key idea is to use refinement types both to express precise functional properties and to decompose specifications into modular subproblems, reducing search. The paper introduces local liquid type checking, including round-trip type checking, liquid abduction for branch conditions, incremental subtyping-constraint solving, and MUSFIX for greatest-fixpoint Horn solving. A prototype synthesizer, SYNQUID, is evaluated on list, tree, sorting, and user-defined data-structure benchmarks, and shown to synthesize more complex verified programs than prior example-based or Hoare-style systems.

papers.title: Raven: Rethinking Automated Assessment for Scratch Programs via Video-Grounded Evaluation
papers.abstract: Raven is an automated assessment framework for Scratch that replaces program-specific state assertions with task-level video generation rules. It combines large language models and video analysis to judge whether a student’s observed visual and interactive behavior satisfies instructor-defined grading criteria, including ask-block interactions. Evaluated on 13 real Scratch assignments with 146 student submissions and compared against Whisker, Raven achieves near-perfect grading performance and stronger robustness to diverse implementations. A classroom study with 30 students and 10 instructors reports strong acceptance and perceived usefulness, suggesting that video-grounded evaluation can improve scalable assessment of open-ended Scratch programs.

papers.title: BLK-Assist: A Methodological Framework for Artist-Led Co-Creation with Generative AI Models
papers.abstract: This paper presents BLK-Assist, a modular framework for artist-specific fine-tuning of diffusion models using parameter-efficient methods. The system is implemented as a case study with a single professional artist’s proprietary corpus and consists of three components: BLK-Conceptor, BLK-Stencil, and BLK-Upscale. The paper documents dataset composition, preprocessing, training configurations, and inference workflows for reproducibility using public models. It argues for a privacy-preserving, consent-based approach to human–AI co-creation that maintains stylistic fidelity to the source corpus and can be adapted for other artists under similar constraints.

papers.title: Enhance Sketch Recognition’s Explainability via Semantic Component-Level Parsing
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a semantic component-level memory module (SCM) embedded in a structured sketch recognition (SSR) network to improve sketch recognition explainability. The method learns memory keys for semantic components and uses them to parse strokes into components, enabling recognition with or without stroke-level semantic labels. With labeled strokes, the model performs simultaneous recognition and segmentation; without them, it uses prior knowledge about which components constitute a category. Experiments on SPG and SketchIME show competitive recognition and segmentation performance and demonstrate that the learned memory keys and component-level parsing make predictions more interpretable.

papers.title: Programming by Sketching for Bit-Streaming Programs
papers.abstract: This paper presents StreamBit, a sketching-based methodology for rapidly developing correct-by-construction, high-performance bit-streaming programs such as ciphers. Programmers write a clean StreamIt reference program and then provide partial implementation sketches; the compiler fills in missing details while ensuring equivalence to the reference. The paper introduces a constraint-based sketch resolver, a sketching language for decomposing permutations and affine functions, and compiler transformations that map stream programs to low-level code. Evaluations include a user study comparing StreamBit to hand-written C and case studies on DES and Serpent, showing that sketched implementations can be highly competitive with optimized public implementations.

papers.title: Precise, Dynamic Information Flow for Database-Backed Applications
papers.abstract: We present dynamic information flow control for database-backed web applications. The approach separates policies from application code and queries, supports existing relational databases, and provides formal guarantees across application and database layers. It introduces faceted databases and a faceted object-relational mapping to encode sensitive values using metadata, along with a λJDB semantics proving termination-insensitive non-interference and policy compliance. The ideas are implemented in Jacqueline, a Python/Django web framework, and evaluated on a course manager, health record system, and conference management system. The system reduces trusted policy code and shows reasonable, often negligible, overheads, with an Early Pruning optimization improving performance.

papers.title: PICACHV: Formally Verified Data Use Policy Enforcement for Secure Data Analytics
papers.abstract: PICACHV is a formally verified runtime monitor for enforcing data use policies in analytical data processing. It models data manipulation at the relational algebra level, defines declassification-aware policies with a security lattice, and mechanizes the semantics and soundness proof in Coq. The system integrates with trusted execution environments to provide verifiable policy compliance in untrusted settings and is implemented in Rust as middleware for analytics frameworks. A prototype integrated into Polars is evaluated on TPC-H and real-world case studies, showing policy enforcement with manageable overhead and practical support for privacy policies such as HIPAA-style redaction, aggregation thresholds, and differential-privacy-style noise addition.

papers.title: Global Stabilization for Causally Consistent Partial Replication
papers.abstract: Causally consistent distributed storage systems often use global stabilization to serialize updates by physical time and compute a Global Stable Time (GST). Existing designs assume full replication and clients confined to one datacenter. This paper develops a framework for general partial replication, where each server stores an arbitrary subset of keys and clients may access and migrate among arbitrary server subsets without extra delays. The authors present a causal-consistency algorithm for partially replicated multi-version key-value stores, define heartbeat-summary based GST computation, and prove its optimality for remote update visibility latency. They also propose migration-delay trade-offs to improve visibility and report simulations showing better performance than GentleRain.

papers.title: Improving Genetic Programming with Behavioral Consistency Measure
papers.abstract: Program synthesis typically evaluates candidate programs by output behavior only, which can mismatch the structural search process. This paper proposes a consistency measure that assesses the information content of intermediate program values, treating them as relevant to future correctness. The measure rewards program prefixes that preserve distinctions needed to produce different outputs and collapse distinctions when outputs should agree. The approach is implemented in both single-objective and multi-objective genetic programming and evaluated on 35 benchmarks across three domains. Results indicate that adding information consistency usually improves the chance of synthesizing the correct program.

papers.title: Lynx: A Programmatic SAT Solver for the RNA-Folding Problem
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Lynx, an incremental programmatic SAT solver that lets users add domain-specific code to a CDCL SAT solver through a callback interface. The paper demonstrates the approach on RNA secondary structure prediction, separating structural from energetic constraints, and reports substantial reductions in memory and runtime compared with standard SAT approaches.

papers.title: Synthesis of Domain Specific CNF Encoders for Bit-Vector Solvers
papers.abstract: The paper presents OptCNF, a system that automatically synthesizes CNF encoders for bit-vector solver terms and then specializes them to benchmark domains. OptCNF uses Sketch-based program synthesis to generate propagation-complete encodings, representative sampling to find recurring term patterns in benchmark DAGs, and OpenTuner to choose the best encoder subset for each domain. The resulting encoders are integrated into CVC4 and evaluated on SMT-COMP 2015 QF_BV benchmarks, where domain-specific versions improve performance and solve more benchmarks than the baseline solver in the tested domains.

papers.title: JSKETCH: Sketching for Java
papers.abstract: JSKETCH is a Java frontend for sketch-based program synthesis using the SKETCH system. It lets programmers write partial Java programs with holes, expression generators, and class generators, and then translates them into SKETCH, synthesizes solutions, and maps results back to Java. The paper describes how JSKETCH models Java object-oriented features such as inheritance, overloading, overriding, inner classes, and dynamic dispatch in a non-object-oriented synthesis language. It also presents example applications including simple arithmetic synthesis, finite automata synthesis, and framework-model synthesis, and discusses implementation details, limitations, and experience using JSKETCH on real examples.

papers.title: Synthesizing Data-structure Manipulations from Storyboards
papers.abstract: We present Storyboard Programming, a synthesis framework for imperative low-level data-structure manipulations. The system takes partial input-output examples together with a high-level control-flow sketch and synthesizes implementations in minutes. It combines constraint-based synthesis with abstract-interpretation-based shape analysis by encoding both the synthesis problem and the abstract semantics as constraints. The framework supports partial specifications via storyboard-style abstractions, fold/unfold predicates for summary nodes, and a loop skeleton for control flow. The paper demonstrates synthesis of linked-list and binary-search-tree manipulations, and also reports results on an And-Inverter Graph data structure.

papers.title: Bridging the Gap Between General-Purpose and Domain-Specific Compilers with Synthesis
papers.abstract: This paper presents Herd, a synthesis-based compiler framework that bridges general-purpose code and domain-specific compilers. Its key idea, Synthesis Enabled Translation (Set), identifies fragments of general-purpose programs that can be provably rewritten into a target DSL, then hands the translated code to domain-specific compilers for aggressive optimization. The paper describes the Herd architecture, including kernel translators, fragment filtering, synthesis of postconditions and invariants, verification, DSL rewriting, and connector code generation. Two example translators are discussed: qbs, which converts Java fragments over persistent data into SQL, and Stng, which converts stencil-style Fortran code into Halide. The paper reports that these translators can improve performance substantially while reducing the need for programmers to rewrite applications into DSLs.

papers.title: Leveraging Sequential Computation for Programming Efficient and Reliable Distributed Systems
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a programming model for distributed systems that treats sequential programs as the core specification of behavior, while separate annotations describe data location, triggers for behavior invocation, and consistency requirements. The compiler is intended to derive distributed implementations, communication, and synchronization from these specifications. The paper illustrates location-dependent types, logical triggers, strong consistency via serialization or locking, dynamic data-structure mapping, verification with SMT and model checking, and optimizations such as communication reduction and trigger elimination.

papers.title: Learning to Acquire Information
papers.abstract: We study active diagnosis, where an agent adaptively selects observations to infer a hidden hypothesis. Directly computing information gain over a complex hypothesis space is intractable, so we assume uniform observation entropy and instead model the conditional distribution of future observations given past ones. Under this assumption, the most informative next query is the one with maximum conditional observation entropy. We implement this with an implication model, a neural network trained only on observation data (not hypothesis labels), and evaluate it on Battleship, sushi preference elicitation, and network fault localization. The method reduces computation by bypassing explicit hypothesis-space inference and performs well against baselines.

papers.title: Modular Synthesis of Sketches Using Models
papers.abstract: This paper presents modular reasoning for sketch-based synthesis using function models. A model includes preprocessing, an uninterpreted function, and a postcondition, enabling decomposition of larger synthesis tasks. The authors define two problems: synthesis with models and synthesis for adherence. They propose Cegis+ for efficiently synthesizing functions that use models, and an approach that eliminates an existentially quantified function to enforce adherence without extra function templates. The methods are implemented in Sketch and evaluated on benchmark problems, showing improved performance over Cegis and prior algorithms.

papers.title: Beyond the Training Distribution: Mapping Generalization Boundaries in Neural Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: Large transformer models perform well on code benchmarks, but their true generalization is obscured by contamination and opaque training data. This paper proposes a controlled program synthesis setting based on an arithmetic context-free grammar, exhaustively enumerating millions of programs and embedding them into semantic and syntactic manifolds. Using these manifolds, the authors define density generalization and support generalization, then train sequence-to-sequence models on differently sampled data splits. Results show that diverse sampling across both semantic and syntactic spaces improves out-of-distribution performance, while extrapolation to novel syntactic structures remains difficult. Scaling compute helps in a strictly log-linear way, and nearest-neighbor proximity strongly predicts success.

papers.title: RVISmith: Fuzzing Compilers for RVV Intrinsics
papers.abstract: RVISmith is a randomized fuzzer for compiler testing of RISC-V Vector Extension (RVV) intrinsics. It generates well-defined C programs containing varied invocation sequences of RVV intrinsics, aiming for high intrinsic coverage, richer sequence variety, and avoidance of known undefined behaviors. The system uses ratio-aligned intrinsic selection, vector-register allocation, intrinsic scheduling, and code generation with explicit handling of RVV-specific undefined behaviors. Evaluated on GCC, LLVM, and XuanTie, RVISmith achieves 11.5× higher intrinsic coverage than the prior RVV fuzzer RIF and uncovers 13 previously unknown compiler bugs, 10 confirmed and 3 fixed by developers.

papers.title: Automatic Generation of Formula Simplifiers based on Conditional Rewrite Rules
papers.abstract: This paper presents Swapper, a system for automatically generating domain-specific formula simplifiers from benchmark corpora. It finds recurring DAG subpatterns by random sampling and clustering, synthesizes conditional rewrite rules using a hybrid of enumerative search and Sketch-based synthesis, compiles them into efficient C++ rewriting code, and auto-tunes rule subsets with OpenTuner. The approach is evaluated on Sketch benchmarks from Storyboard, Query Extraction, AutoGrader, and SyGuS. The generated simplifiers reduce DAG sizes and improve solving time over both the baseline and hand-coded Sketch simplifier, while also showing strong domain specificity.

papers.title: Results and Analysis of SyGuS-Comp’15
papers.abstract: This paper reports and analyzes the 2015 Syntax-Guided Synthesis Competition (SyGuS-Comp’15). It describes the SyGuS formalism, the competition’s general, conditional linear arithmetic (LIA), and invariant synthesis (INV) tracks, the benchmark categories and solver configurations, and the experimental setup on StarExec. The paper summarizes solver performance across tracks and categories, compares solution times and expression sizes, and discusses correlations between benchmark features and solver strengths. It concludes with observations about solver behavior, especially the advantages of CVC4-1.5-SYGUS on single-invocation problems and ICE-DT on invariant synthesis benchmarks.

papers.title: SyGuS-Comp 2016: Results and Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper reports the results of SyGuS-Comp 2016, the third Syntax-Guided Synthesis competition. It summarizes the competition’s tracks—general, conditional linear integer arithmetic, invariant synthesis, and a new programming-by-example track—along with benchmark suites, participating solvers, and experimental setup. The paper analyzes solver performance by number of benchmarks solved, time to solve, and expression size, and compares the behavior of CVC4-1.5.1, CVC4-1.5, EUSolver, ENUMERATIVE, ICE-DT, Sketch-AC, STOCHASTIC, and others across categories such as compiler optimizations, arrays, hackers’ delight, integers, multiple functions, and PBE strings/bitvectors.

papers.title: Learning to Infer Graphics Programs from Hand-Drawn Images
papers.abstract: We present a system that converts simple hand drawings into graphics programs in a subset of LaTeX. It first infers a low-level specification of drawing commands from an image using a convolutional network and stochastic search, then synthesizes a structured program with loops, conditionals, and reflections from that spec. The approach uses neural proposals, Sequential Monte Carlo, a learned similarity model for hand drawings, and program synthesis in a restricted DSL. The resulting programs support error correction, comparison of drawings by high-level structure, and extrapolation of repetitive figures.

papers.title: (Un)Decidability Results for Word Equations with Length and Regular Expression Constraints
papers.abstract: The paper proves new decidability and undecidability results for satisfiability and validity problems over string formulas combining word equations, length constraints, and regular-expression membership. It shows that validity for ∀∃ sentences over positive word equations is undecidable, via reduction from two-counter machines, and that a conditional solved-form assumption yields decidability for quantifier-free word equations with length constraints. It also proves decidability for quantifier-free formulas with word equations in regular solved form, length constraints, and regular-expression membership. The work connects these results to practical string-analysis and bug-finding tools such as Kudzu and Kaluza.

papers.title: Report of the HPC Correctness Summit
papers.abstract: This report summarizes a summit on HPC correctness held in Washington, DC, on Jan. 25–26, 2017. It argues that exascale-era heterogeneity, massive scale, non-intuitive behaviors, cognitive overload, new scalable algorithms, and community unpreparedness make correctness a pressing HPC problem. The report surveys specification and verification approaches, state-of-the-art testing, static and dynamic analysis, debugging, anomaly detection, and certification. It recommends short-, medium-, and long-term research foci, including tool integration, bug repositories, verification of runtime systems and libraries, numerical specification, and better support for floating-point reasoning and parallel debugging. It also proposes moonshot projects such as certified molecular dynamics, multiphysics, and verified compiler/runtime components, plus an HPC verification competition.

papers.title: Synthesis of Recursive ADT Transformations from Reusable Templates
papers.abstract: We present SyntRec, a synthesis system for recursive transformations on algebraic data types. Its key idea is polymorphic synthesis constructs that make syntactic templates reusable across many tasks while retaining the scalability benefits of template-guided synthesis. The paper also introduces inductive decomposition, an optimization that can eliminate recursive calls during CEGIS when the specification has an inductive structure. Implemented on top of Sketch, SyntRec supports rich semantic specifications and can synthesize desugaring, list, tree, and AST transformations from a small library of generic templates. Experiments on 23 benchmarks show substantial performance gains over unoptimized synthesis and demonstrate synthesis of nontrivial tasks such as Church encodings and type-constraint generation.

metadata_evidence.evidence: Synthesis of Recursive ADT Transformations from Reusable Templates
Jeevana Priya Inala1, Nadia Polikarpova1, Xiaokang Qiu2, Benjamin S. Lerner3, and Armando Solar-Lezama1

Abstract. Recent work has proposed a promising approach to improving scalability of program synthesis by allowing the user to supply a syntactic template that constrains the space of potential programs.
Our first contribution is a new approach to making syntactic templates highly reusable by relying on polymorphic synthesis constructs (PSCs).
Our second contribution is a new optimization called inductive decomposition, which achieves asymptotic improvements in synthesis times for large and non-trivial ADT transformations.
We implemented these ideas in a tool called SyntRec, which is built on top of the open source Sketch synthesis platform [19].

papers.title: JSKETCH: Sketching for Java
papers.abstract: JSKETCH is a tool that brings sketch-based synthesis to Java. Given a partial Java program with holes, expression generators, and class generators, it translates the problem into SKETCH, synthesizes a solution, and then maps the result back to executable Java. The paper describes the core translation challenges posed by Java’s object-oriented features, including inheritance, method overloading/overriding, inner and anonymous classes, and shows examples such as simple arithmetic synthesis and automaton synthesis. It also reports experience using JSKETCH to synthesize framework models through PASKET.

papers.title: One Tool, Many Languages: Language-Parametric Transformation with Incremental Parametric Syntax
papers.abstract: The paper presents Cubix, a Haskell framework for source-to-source transformations that work across multiple real programming languages. Its core idea is incremental parametric syntax (IPS), which combines generic and language-specific syntax so transformations can operate on shared fragments while preserving source structure. The authors implement IPS for C, Java, JavaScript, Lua, and Python, and show language-parametric refactoring and analysis-adjacent transformations such as declaration hoisting, test coverage insertion, three-address-code conversion, and a whole-program interprocedural plumbing transformation. Evaluation includes compiler test-suite validation and a human readability study, supporting claims that the approach preserves readable output and handles language corner cases.

This paper presents the first work that builds source-to-source transformations that run on multiple real languages.
We have implemented incremental parametric syntax in a Haskell framework called Cubix, and implemented support for 5 languages: C, Java, JavaScript, Lua, and Python.

We present the concept of parametric syntax, which allows the user to define a family of representations specific to different languages, but source-to-source transformations that can run on many of them.
We develop the concept of sort injections, which modularly specify which edges may be in an AST, and hence provide a typed and modular way to intermix language-specific and generic fragments.

papers.title: Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types
papers.abstract: We present a method for synthesizing recursive functions that provably satisfy specifications expressed as polymorphic refinement types. The approach exploits the expressiveness and decidability of reification types to support modular, type-directed synthesis, including decomposition of specifications across subterms. The core technical contribution is local liquid type checking, which combines round-trip type checking, liquid abduction for conditional guards and pattern matching, incremental constraint solving, and a greatest-fixpoint Horn solver called MUSFIX. A prototype synthesizer, SYNQUID, is evaluated on a broad benchmark set and shown to synthesize programs manipulating lists, trees, and data structures with complex invariants, often outperforming prior synthesis systems and requiring more concise specifications.

papers.title: Liquid Information Flow Control
papers.abstract: We present Lifty, a domain-specific language for data-centric applications that statically enforces declarative, data-dependent information-flow policies using liquid types. Programmers annotate sensitive sources with policies; the type checker verifies code against those policies and reports leaks at compile time. When verification fails, Lifty can localize the leak and synthesize a provably correct repair by guarding the unsafe access and redacting with a designated safe fallback. The paper describes the TIO security monad, a liquid-type-based IFC encoding, a type-driven localization and patch synthesis algorithm, and an implementation evaluated on microbenchmarks and case studies including conference management, health records, and course management systems.

papers.title: Learning to Acquire Information
papers.abstract: We study active diagnosis, where an agent chooses informative observations to infer a hidden hypothesis. The paper shows that under a uniform observation entropy assumption, the best next observation can be selected by maximizing the conditional entropy of the observation itself rather than entropy over the hypothesis space. This enables an implication model that predicts future observation outcomes directly from past observations, avoiding explicit hypothesis modeling. The implication model is trained on observation data alone using a neural network with masked inputs, and is used for adaptive observation collection. Experiments on Battleship, sushi preference elicitation, and network fault localization show improved performance over baseline methods.

papers.title: sk_p: a neural program corrector for MOOCs
papers.abstract: We present a technique for automatic program correction in MOOCs that can fix syntactic and semantic errors without manual, problem-specific strategies. Given an incorrect student program, the system generates candidate corrections from a learned distribution and checks them against a test suite. It treats programs syntactically as token sequences and uses a modified seq2seq neural network to predict missing or replacement statements from local program context. Experiments on seven Python assignments from MITx 6.00x show that the system corrects 29% of incorrect submissions and outperforms a prior autograder-based approach on several benchmarks.

papers.title: Precise, Dynamic Information Flow for Database-Backed Applications
papers.abstract: We present dynamic information flow control for database-backed web applications. The approach factors information-flow policies out of application code and database queries, and provides formal guarantees across both layers. The paper defines a policy-agnostic programming model, faceted databases using relational storage and metadata, and the λJDB core semantics with proofs of termination-insensitive non-interference and policy compliance. A Python/Django implementation called Jacqueline demonstrates the approach on course management, health records, and conference management systems, with reduced policy code and reasonable overheads. The paper also introduces Early Pruning to improve performance by eliminating unnecessary facet exploration once the viewer is known.

papers.title: Automated Feedback Generation for Introductory Programming Assignments
papers.abstract: We present a method for automatically providing feedback for introductory programming assignments. The approach requires a reference implementation and an error model of likely student mistakes, then computes minimal corrections to an incorrect submission. A correction-rule language is introduced and translated into a synthesis problem by reducing error-model application to sketch completion. The implementation supports a substantial subset of Python, including higher-order functions and list comprehensions, and uses constraint-based synthesis with a minimum-change objective. Evaluated on thousands of real student submissions from MIT 6.00 and 6.00x, the system provides feedback for about 65% of incorrect solutions, often within seconds.

papers.title: Inferring SQL Queries Using Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: The paper presents QBS, a synthesis-based compiler analysis for converting imperative application code that uses ORM libraries into equivalent SQL queries. QBS infers loop invariants and postconditions in a theory of ordered relations, enabling precise reasoning about both contents and record order. The inferred predicates are translated into SQL if they are valid and translatable. The authors evaluate a prototype on 40 real-world Java/Hibernate code fragments from two open-source applications, showing that QBS can infer selections, projections, joins, and aggregates more broadly than prior query-extraction work.

papers.title: Using Program Synthesis for Social Recommendations
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid approach for social event recommendation in LifeJoin, combining program synthesis with machine learning. The goal is to learn each user’s interests from liked and disliked events while producing decomposable boolean predicates that can be pushed to mobile devices for data collection and filtering. The method uses Sketch to synthesize candidate interest functions and an SVM to weight their predicates, enabling active learning, robustness to noisy labels, and interpretable models. Experiments on synthetic LifeJoin data show improved classification accuracy and much faster feature encoding than traditional feature-selection baselines, while also yielding human-readable decomposable models.

papers.title: Capturing the Future by Replaying the Past
papers.abstract: This functional pearl presents thermometer continuations: a way to implement delimited continuations using only exceptions and state by replaying a computation from the start and guiding it with recorded effects. The paper develops replay-based nondeterminism as a warm-up, then generalizes the idea to delimited control and combines it with Filinski’s monadic reflection to obtain direct-style implementations of arbitrary monadic effects. It also discusses optimizations, benchmarks, limitations around side effects and typing, and why the construction does not contradict prior impossibility results about exceptions, state, and continuations.

papers.title: Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: Program synthesis often uses input-output examples as constraints, but large example sets can make solving slow and memory-intensive. The paper proposes an iterative method that selects a small representative subset of examples using a neural network to estimate how probable unchosen examples are conditioned on the chosen subset, then greedily adds the least probable example. The selected subset is used directly or as an initialization for CEGIS, improving scalability while aiming to preserve correctness. Experiments on ordering synthesis, DFA synthesis, and programmatic drawing show that the method usually finds representative subsets and can improve synthesis time and stability compared with random selection and several CEGIS baselines.

papers.title: SyGuS-Comp 2017: Results and Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper reports and analyzes the results of the 2017 Syntax-Guided Synthesis Competition (SyGuS-Comp). It describes the benchmark sets, participating solvers, experimental setup, and performance across five tracks: general, conditional linear integer arithmetic, invariant generation, and programming-by-example for bitvectors and strings. The report compares solvers by number solved, time to solve, uniqueness, and expression size, and highlights that 65% of the new benchmarks were solved. It also summarizes which benchmark categories remained challenging, including multiple-function synthesis, varying-parameter specifications, let expressions, very general grammars, and partial specifications.

papers.title: ReaS: Combining Numerical Optimization with SAT Solving
papers.abstract: ReaS combines numerical optimization with SAT solving for program synthesis over mixed discrete and floating-point computation. It smooths Boolean structure to make programs end-to-end differentiable, relaxes Boolean unknowns to reals, and then uses a SAT solver to fix Boolean decisions and steer numerical search away from local optima. Implemented on top of Sketch, ReaS synthesizes controllers for hybrid systems such as lane changing, quadcopter control, parallel parking, and thermostat control, solving benchmarks that prior SMT and smoothing-based approaches could not.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Network Judgments via Minimal, Stable, and Symbolic Corrections
papers.abstract: We present an algorithm that generates minimal, stable, and symbolic corrections to an input so a ReLU neural network changes its output. The method is intended as actionable feedback for binary judgment problems, where a negative decision should be explained by how to obtain a positive one. It works by solving a series of linear constraint satisfaction problems, growing verified linear regions around an initial concrete correction and then inferring a convex symbolic correction. The approach is evaluated on mortgage underwriting, first-order theorem proving, and drawing recognition, and it produces useful corrections in practice.

papers.title: The Three Pillars of Machine Programming
papers.abstract: This position paper presents a framework for machine programming built around three pillars: intention, invention, and adaptation. It argues that advances in natural-input interfaces, program synthesis, machine learning, compiler optimization, and automated repair can move software creation and maintenance from humans to machines. The paper surveys representative systems in each pillar, discusses their interactions using verified lifting as an example, and emphasizes the role of data from code repositories, natural-language sources, and synthetic data in enabling machine programming systems.

papers.title: Verifiable Reinforcement Learning via Policy Extraction
papers.abstract: We present VIPER, a policy-extraction approach for learning decision tree policies from deep reinforcement learning oracles so that the resulting policies are efficient to verify. VIPER extends DAGGER by using the oracle’s Q-function to focus learning on critical states, producing much smaller trees than standard imitation learning. The paper shows how extracted decision trees can be verified for robustness, correctness, and stability, and demonstrates the approach on symbolic Atari Pong, a toy Pong game, cart-pole, and half-cheetah. In each case, the extracted tree matches the oracle’s performance while enabling substantially more scalable verification than neural-network policies.

papers.title: Delta-Decision Procedures for Exists-Forall Problems over the Reals
papers.abstract: We propose δ-complete decision procedures for satisfiability of nonlinear SMT problems over the reals with universal quantification and nonlinear functions. The approach integrates interval constraint propagation, counterexample-guided synthesis, and numerical optimization inside a branch-and-prune framework. A key contribution is double-sided error control for counterexample generation, which preserves δ-completeness, along with locally optimized counterexamples to improve pruning. The paper proves δ-completeness for CNF∀ formulas over computable real functions and demonstrates effectiveness on global optimization and Lyapunov function synthesis benchmarks.

papers.title: Probabilistic Verification of Fairness Properties via Concentration
papers.abstract: We present VeriFair, a scalable algorithm for verifying fairness specifications of machine learning models. The method uses sampling plus adaptive concentration inequalities to obtain probabilistic soundness and precision guarantees, allowing it to keep sampling until it can decide a fairness property with a chosen error bound. The paper formalizes several fairness notions, including demographic parity, equal opportunity, and path-specific causal fairness, and shows how to verify them from black-box access to classifiers and population models. Experiments show that VeriFair scales to larger models than prior work, including deep recurrent neural networks, and outperforms the FairSquare verifier on benchmark instances.

papers.title: Soft Constraints for Inference with Declarative Knowledge
papers.abstract: We present predicate exchange, a likelihood-free inference method for conditioning probabilistic models on declarative predicates. The approach relaxes Boolean predicates into soft predicates in [0,1] using a temperature-controlled soft Boolean algebra, then combines this relaxation with replica exchange Markov chain Monte Carlo to obtain asymptotically exact samples from the unrelaxed model. The paper describes the measure-theoretic basis for conditioning on predicates, a lightweight implementation over stochastic simulation programs, and experiments on truncated Gaussians, equality constraints between random variables, and glycemic forecasting.

papers.title: Learning to Infer Program Sketches
papers.abstract: We introduce SKETCHADAPT, a neuro-symbolic program synthesis system that learns an intermediate sketch representation between neural pattern recognition and symbolic search. The model is trained self-supervised to choose sketches that can be efficiently completed within a time budget, allowing it to dynamically vary how much of a program is proposed by a neural generator versus filled in by enumerative synthesis. Experiments on list processing, string transformations, and AlgoLisp description-to-code tasks show that the approach matches or exceeds neural baselines on familiar tasks while improving generalization and data efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art performance on AlgoLisp.

papers.title: Deductive Optimization of Relational Data Storage
papers.abstract: Castor is a domain-specific language and compiler for static databases that combines query compilation with deductive synthesis of specialized data layouts. It extends relational algebra with layout operators to represent row stores, nested layouts, and indexes, and applies semantics-preserving transformations to jointly optimize query execution and storage structure. The system compiles serializable layouts to compact binary representations and generates LLVM-based query code. Experiments on TPC-H-derived benchmarks show Castor can match or outperform a state-of-the-art in-memory compiled database system while using substantially less memory.

papers.title: The Random Conditional Distribution For Higher-Order Probabilistic Inference
papers.abstract: The paper introduces random conditional distributions, a higher-order probabilistic construct for representing uncertainty over distributional properties such as expectation, variance, and entropy. It formalizes the construct in measure-theoretic probability and integrates it into the probabilistic programming language Omega, where distributional operators can be lifted to random conditional distributions. The approach enables compact expression of distributional inference tasks that are awkward in existing probabilistic languages. The paper motivates the idea with applications in algorithmic fairness and robustness, presents syntax and semantics for Omega, and evaluates expressiveness against WebPPL. Case studies show how Omega can be used to infer fair classifiers and more robust classifiers by conditioning on distributional properties.

papers.title: Write, Execute, Assess: Program Synthesis with a REPL
papers.abstract: We present a neural program synthesis approach that integrates writing, executing, and assessing code through a REPL to search the semantic space of programs. A learned policy proposes code actions, and a learned value function estimates the likelihood that partial programs will succeed. At test time, the method combines these models with Sequential Monte Carlo search, enabling branching, pruning, and resampling of candidate programs. The approach is evaluated on two domains: synthesizing text-editing programs and inferring 2D and 3D graphics programs. Results show that the REPL-based, value-guided search improves reliability and efficiency over policy-only and no-REPL baselines.

papers.title: Learning Compositional Rules via Neural Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: Humans learn compositional rules from few examples, but neural sequence models often fail to generalize systematically. This paper presents a neuro-symbolic program synthesis approach that induces explicit rule systems from support examples, then symbolically applies the learned grammar to new inputs. The model encodes input-output examples with BiLSTMs, decodes a candidate interpretation grammar with attention, and uses search plus symbolic checking to find a grammar consistent with the support set. Across MiniSCAN, SCAN, and few-shot number-word learning, the method outperforms meta-learning and other baselines, achieving strong or perfect generalization in several settings and showing improved out-of-distribution behavior.

papers.title: DreamCoder: Growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
papers.abstract: DreamCoder is a program-induction system that learns to solve tasks by growing both a symbolic domain-specific language and a neural recognition model. It alternates wake phases, where programs are searched for task solutions, with two sleep phases: abstraction, which compresses recurrent program fragments into new library primitives, and dreaming, which trains the recognizer on replayed and imagined tasks. The paper demonstrates results across eight domains, including list processing, text editing, graphics, tower building, regex learning, symbolic regression, and learning of physical laws and recursive programming idioms. DreamCoder discovers interpretable abstractions such as map, filter, vector operations, and higher-order recursive patterns, improving both sample efficiency and search efficiency while producing human-readable hierarchical representations.

papers.title: Neurosymbolic Transformers for Multi-Agent Communication
papers.abstract: We study learning communication structures for cooperative multi-agent planning while minimizing communication degree. The method trains a transformer policy as an oracle, synthesizes a programmatic communication policy that hardens the transformer’s soft attention into sparse hard decisions, and then retrains the transformer with these hard attentions. Communication is measured by the maximum degree of the communication graph, capturing bandwidth limits. Experiments on multi-agent formation and cooperative navigation tasks show near-oracle task performance with substantially reduced communication.

papers.title: Program Synthesis Guided Reinforcement Learning for Partially Observed Environments
papers.abstract: We propose model predictive program synthesis (MPPS) for program-guided reinforcement learning in partially observed environments. MPPS uses a conditional generative model to hallucinate the unobserved parts of the world, then synthesizes a high-level program that maximizes the probability of success across sampled hallucinations, and finally executes the corresponding learned options. The method reduces the need for users to handwrite task-specific programs and handles uncertainty via replanning. Experiments on 2D craft, box-world, and an ant-based craft transfer task show large gains over non-program-guided baselines and performance close to an oracle with ground-truth programs.

papers.title: Safe Human-Interactive Control via Shielding
papers.abstract: Ensuring safety for human-interactive robotics is important due to the potential for human injury. The paper proposes safety modulo fault, where the designer specifies robot backup actions that humans are expected to anticipate and human backup action sets that humans may take to avoid accidents. Using abstract interpretation, the method overapproximates reachable states and builds a model-predictive shield that overrides an arbitrary controller only when needed. The approach is evaluated in simulation with both simulated and real human participants, showing improved safety while retaining much of the performance of the base controller.

papers.title: JoinABLe: Learning Bottom-up Assembly of Parametric CAD Joints
papers.abstract: JoinABLe is a learning-based method for automatically assembling pairs of CAD parts by predicting parametric joints from weak supervision in standard parametric CAD files. The method operates on B-Rep graph representations, predicts joint axes with a graph neural network, and then searches for joint pose parameters using a neurally guided optimization procedure. It does not require object class labels, part class labels, or human guidance. The paper introduces the Fusion 360 Gallery assembly dataset, which contains assemblies, joints, contacts, holes, and assembly graph structure. Experiments show that JoinABLe outperforms several point-cloud and B-Rep baselines and approaches human CAD expert performance on joint axis prediction.

papers.title: Metric Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: We present metric program synthesis, a domain-agnostic programming-by-example technique that relaxes observational equivalence into observational similarity. Programs are clustered using a distance metric to build an approximate finite tree automaton (XFTA) representing close candidates, then a greedy extraction step and a distance-guided repair step search for an exact solution. The approach is instantiated in inverse CSG, regular expression synthesis, and tower building, and implemented in SyMetric. Experiments show that SyMetric outperforms domain-agnostic baselines based on equivalence reduction and is competitive with domain-specific synthesizers.
