papers.title: Searching Entangled Program Spaces
papers.abstract: The paper introduces equality-constrained tree automata (ECTAs) for compactly representing program spaces with entangled subterms, where choices are not independent. It presents static reduction to prune impossible transitions and dynamic reduction to delay constrained choices during enumeration. The authors formalize acyclic and cyclic ECTAs, prove soundness and termination properties, and show encodings for SAT and type-driven program synthesis. They implement the approach in Haskell as ecta and use it to build Hectare, a type-driven synthesizer that outperforms Hoogle+ on benchmark suites.

papers.title: SPARLING: End-to-End Spatial Concept Learning via Extremely Sparse Activations
papers.abstract: This paper studies when sparse local latent intermediate variables (“motifs”) can be recovered from end-to-end supervision alone. It proves a Motif Identifiability Theorem showing that under non-overlapping motifs, motif sufficiency, and alpha-motif-necessity, low end-to-end error implies low motif error up to simple transformations. The paper also introduces SPARLING, a sparsity-enforcing training method based on a spatial sparsity layer with adaptive thresholding and sparsity annealing. Experiments on synthetic DIGITCIRCLE, LATEX-OCR, and AUDIOMNISTSEQUENCE tasks show that extremely sparse intermediate activations can recover motifs accurately without direct motif supervision, and that extreme sparsity is important for good motif identification.

papers.title: CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
papers.abstract: We present CRUXEval, a benchmark of 800 short Python functions with paired inputs and outputs, designed to test two tasks: output prediction and input prediction. The paper describes a generate-and-filter construction pipeline using Code Llama to create candidate programs, then selecting simple, low-computation examples. The benchmark is used to evaluate 20 code models, showing that strong performance on HumanEval does not necessarily transfer to execution reasoning. GPT-4 performs best, especially with chain-of-thought prompting, while open models lag behind. Fine-tuning and CoT improve scores but do not solve the benchmark, and the paper analyzes qualitative failure modes on simple programs.

papers.title: The Counterfeit Conundrum: Can Code Language Models Grasp the Nuances of Their Incorrect Generations?
papers.abstract: This paper studies “counterfeit” code samples: incorrect programs sampled from code language models that still pass weak correctness checks. Using HumanEval, LeetCode, and ODEX, the authors evaluate models on correctness checking, execution prediction, and repair. They find that most models, especially open-source ones, struggle to distinguish counterfeit from correct code, often predict counterfeit execution as if the code were correct, and frequently repair counterfeit programs no better than simple resampling. The paper also reports that counterfeit difficulty is not strongly tied to problem difficulty or model strength, and that models’ own counterfeits are confusing to themselves and to other models alike.

papers.title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
papers.abstract: LiveCodeBench is a continuously updated, contamination-free benchmark for evaluating large language models on code. It collects 511 contest problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces released from May 2023 to May 2024, and evaluates models across four scenarios: code generation, self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction. The benchmark uses release dates to support time-segmented evaluation and reduce contamination from training data overlap. The authors report results for 18 base models and 34 instruction-tuned models, finding evidence of contamination in some models, overfitting to HumanEval, and large performance gaps between open and closed models. The benchmark also provides a toolkit and prompts for adding new scenarios.

papers.title: When Do Skills Help Reinforcement Learning? A Theoretical Analysis of Temporal Abstractions
papers.abstract: We study when temporal abstractions (skills) help reinforcement learning in deterministic sparse-reward MDPs with finite action spaces. The paper defines p-learning difficulty and p-exploration difficulty and shows they correlate with sample complexity across several RL algorithms and environments. It then introduces incompressibility measures for solution trajectories and proves lower bounds relating these measures to how much skills can improve learning and exploration. The results imply that skills are more likely to help in environments whose solutions are more compressible, that skills tend to help exploration more than learning from experience, and that unexpressive skills such as macroactions can sometimes worsen performance. Empirical tests on grid worlds, puzzles, and Rubik’s cube variants support the theory and connect the measures to skill-discovery objectives.

papers.title: MeMo: Meaningful, Modular Controllers via Noise Injection
papers.abstract: MeMo learns meaningful modular controllers for robots built from repeated assemblies. Starting from a single robot and expert controller, it trains a boss controller and shared assembly-specific modules with a noise-injection objective that balances behavior cloning and invariance to perturbations, encouraging modules to take responsibility for coordination within each assembly. The learned modules can be reused to transfer control to new morphologies built from the same parts, and also to new tasks. Experiments in locomotion and grasping show improved transfer efficiency over graph neural network and Transformer baselines. Ablations indicate that the noise-injection objective is key and that it reduces the effective dimensionality of the boss signal.

papers.title: MathDSL: A Domain-Specific Language for Concise Mathematical Solutions Via Program Synthesis
papers.abstract: We present MathDSL, a domain-specific language for linear-equation solving that, when used with DreamCoder and Stitch, produces more accurate and more concise solutions than reinforcement-learning baselines such as ConPoLe and Lemma. The paper introduces an AST-based conciseness metric and shows that MathDSL can induce reusable abstractions that yield human-interpretable solution strategies. Experiments on a modified Cognitive Tutor Algebra dataset indicate higher accuracy and improved conciseness, including after de-duplication of DreamCoder-generated solution steps. The authors also test DreamCoder with ConPoLe-style and Lemma-style action spaces as DSLs to show the gains come from MathDSL’s design rather than DreamCoder alone.

papers.title: Randomly Sampled Language Reasoning Problems Elucidate Limitations of In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: The paper studies in-context learning on very simple but randomly sampled language reasoning tasks built from 3-state deterministic finite automata (DFAs). By sampling novel languages rather than using canonical tasks, the authors aim to isolate novelty from world modeling and parametric knowledge. They evaluate sequence completion and transducer-style next-token prediction across many LLMs and compare them with n-gram and brute-force DFA baselines. The main finding is that LLMs generally underperform simple n-gram models on these unfamiliar language tasks, including in chain-of-thought settings, suggesting limited ability to generalize to entirely novel language reasoning problems.

papers.title: VLMATERIAL: Procedural Material Generation with Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: We present VLMATERIAL, a method for generating Blender procedural materials from a single input image by fine-tuning a large vision-language model to output Python programs that transpile into editable shader node graphs. To address the scarcity of training data, we build and release an open-source Blender procedural material dataset and substantially expand it using program-structure augmentation with a large language model plus node-parameter augmentation. We further refine predicted materials with a gradient-free MCMC-based local parameter search. Experiments on synthetic Blender materials, out-of-distribution Substance materials, and real photographs show that the proposed approach outperforms prior methods in perceptual similarity and program validity, while preserving editability.

papers.title: MIMEQA: Towards Socially-Intelligent Nonverbal Foundation Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces MIMEQA, a video question-answering benchmark built from mime performances to evaluate socially intelligent nonverbal understanding in multimodal models. The dataset contains 101 videos and 806 verified question-answer pairs spanning grounding of imagined objects, scene-level reasoning, and global-level social cognition such as theory of mind and social judgment. Experiments show that current VideoLLMs perform poorly on MIMEQA, with large gaps versus human performance, especially on grounding imagined objects. The authors also analyze failure modes, test fine-tuning and pose-based inputs, and study transfer to related social reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Challenges and Paths Towards AI for Software Engineering
papers.abstract: AI for software engineering has recently made notable progress, but many bottlenecks remain before automated software engineering can reach high levels of usefulness and autonomy. This paper presents a structured taxonomy of AI-for-software-engineering tasks beyond code generation, summarizes nine cross-cutting challenges such as evaluation, tool use, human-AI collaboration, long-horizon planning, large context, semantic codebase understanding, low-resource languages, API version changes, and high logical complexity, and outlines promising research directions spanning data collection, training, and inference-time methods.

papers.title: Using Program Analysis to Improve Database Applications
papers.abstract: This article describes three projects that improve database application performance by co-optimizing application/runtime systems with the DBMS. QBS uses program synthesis and Hoare-style reasoning to translate imperative code fragments into SQL queries. PYXIS uses static dependency analysis and workload-sensitive program partitioning to split application logic between application and database servers. SLOTH uses extended lazy evaluation to batch database queries and reduce network round trips. Across real-world Java applications, these techniques yield substantial speedups while preserving a high-level programming model.

papers.title: An empirical study of adaptive concretization for parallel program synthesis
papers.abstract: Adaptive concretization is a program synthesis technique that combines explicit and symbolic search and parallelizes well. This paper systematically evaluates design choices in the algorithm, including a new smooth probability function for concretizing unknowns, the degree-search procedure, the Wilcoxon test threshold, and the influence-weight ratio for boolean nodes. Across 31 benchmarks, the authors find that the smooth probability function performs similarly to the earlier discontinuous version, the expected running time forms a vee around an optimal concretization degree, and moderate threshold and weight choices are robust. The results support adaptive concretization as an effective and relatively insensitive strategy for parallel program synthesis.

papers.title: NeSyCat: A Monad-Based Categorical Semantics of the Neurosymbolic ULLER Framework
papers.abstract: ULLER provides a unified first-order logic syntax for neurosymbolic systems, but its classical, fuzzy, and probabilistic semantics are separately specified and partly non-modular. This paper presents NeSyCat, a monad-based categorical semantics that treats these semantics as instances of one framework. The approach separates syntax, interpretation, and semantic evaluation, supports modular translation between semantics, and extends naturally to continuous probability via categorical probability monads such as the Giry monad on measurable spaces. The paper develops set-based and categorical NeSy frameworks, defines a truth-value algebra (2Mon-BLat), gives inductive Tarskian semantics for ordinary and computational formulas, and illustrates classical, three-valued, distributional, and Logic Tensor Network semantics. It also relates the framework to weighted model counting and integration, discusses implementations in Python and Haskell, and sketches extensions for infinite domains and continuous distributions.

papers.title: Compact LLM Deployment and World Model Assisted Offloading in Mobile Edge Computing
papers.abstract: This paper studies compact large language model deployment and world-model-assisted inference offloading in mobile edge computing. It proposes an edge compact LLM deployment framework that combines structured pruning, knowledge distillation, and low-bit quantization to create device-specific models, evaluated with accessibility, energy consumption, hallucination rate, and generalization accuracy. The paper then formulates a joint offloading and power-control optimization problem that minimizes long-term inference latency under energy budgets and accuracy/hallucination constraints. To solve it in unknown dynamic networks, the authors develop a world model-PPO algorithm that augments on-policy PPO with a recurrent world model for improved value targets and imagination rollouts. Experiments on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Mistral-12B show strong compression, lower energy use, and improved convergence and latency relative to baselines.

papers.title: Probabilistic Verification of Fairness Properties via Concentration
papers.abstract: The paper presents VeriFair, a probabilistic verification algorithm for fairness specifications of machine learning models. It uses adaptive concentration inequalities and sampling to estimate conditional expectations and decide fairness properties with high-probability guarantees. The method is designed to scale to large black-box models, including deep recurrent neural networks, and is shown to outperform the FairSquare verifier on benchmark instances. The paper formalizes several fairness notions, including demographic parity, equal opportunity, path-specific causal fairness, and an individual-fairness variant, and proves probabilistic soundness, precision, and near-certain termination except in pathological cases.

papers.title: Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning
papers.abstract: This paper presents corpus-guided top-down synthesis (CTS) for library learning: a branch-and-bound method that directly synthesizes reusable function abstractions from a corpus of programs. CTS uses syntactic matching between partial abstractions and corpus subtrees to prune the search space and guide search toward abstractions that maximize a utility objective, instantiated here as program compression. The implementation, Stitch, learns libraries comparable or better than prior deductive library-learning systems while using far less time and memory, and it scales to corpora of hundreds of complex programs. The paper also shows that CTS degrades gracefully under early stopping and can be combined with deductive rewrite systems such as version spaces to recover some higher-order abstractions.

papers.title: Deductive Optimization of Relational Data Storage
papers.abstract: Castor is a domain-specific language and compiler for static databases that jointly optimizes query execution and physical data layout. It extends relational algebra with layout operators, deductive equivalence-preserving transformations, and a type-driven layout compiler that serializes specialized data structures and generates LLVM-based query code. The system can express row stores, clustered indexes, nested layouts, hash indexes, and ordered indexes, enabling aggressive precomputation and layout specialization. Experiments on TPC-H-derived workloads show competitive performance with Hyper while using significantly less memory, and better scalability than Cozy on larger queries.

papers.title: Searching Entangled Program Spaces
papers.abstract: The paper introduces equality-constrained tree automata (ECTAs) for compactly representing program spaces with entangled subterms, where choices in different parts of a term are not independent. It develops static reduction to prune impossible transitions before search and dynamic reduction to defer constrained choices during enumeration. The paper formalizes acyclic and cyclic ECTAs, proves correctness and termination properties, and shows encodings for SAT and type-driven synthesis. An implementation in Haskell, ecta, is used to build Hectare, a type-driven Haskell synthesizer that outperforms Hoogle+ on benchmarks.

papers.title: Automatically Deriving Control-Flow Graph Generators from Operational Semantics
papers.abstract: The paper develops a theory connecting operational semantics to control-flow graphs (CFGs) and uses it to automatically synthesize CFG generators from a language’s small-step semantics. It introduces an algorithm that converts structural operational semantics into a phased abstract machine, then applies abstract rewriting plus abstraction and projection choices to generate either interpreted CFGs or standalone syntax-directed CFG-generator code. The approach supports multiple CFG styles, proves correspondence between generated graphs and the source semantics, and includes an automated termination proof for compiled-mode generators. The implementation, Mandate, is demonstrated on several languages including IMP, Tiger, and MITScript, and its generated CFGs are used to build static analyses.

papers.title: One Tool, Many Languages: Language-Parametric Transformation with Incremental Parametric Syntax
papers.abstract: We present incremental parametric syntax (IPS), a representation for source-to-source program transformations that can be configured across multiple programming languages while preserving output readability and structure. The approach combines language-specific syntax frontends with generic fragments and sort injections, implemented in the Cubix Haskell framework. Cubix supports C, Java, JavaScript, Lua, and Python, and is used to build several multi-language transformations including hoisting, test coverage insertion, three-address code conversion, and a whole-program interprocedural plumbing refactoring. The paper evaluates readability with a human study and correctness using compiler test suites, showing that the transformations can remain readable and handle language corner cases.

papers.title: Capturing the Future by Replaying the Past
papers.abstract: This paper presents thermometer continuations, a replay-based way to implement delimited continuations using only exceptions and state. The key idea is to re-execute a computation from the beginning while recording enough information to guide replay so the computation reaches the same continuation point. The paper first develops replay-based nondeterminism as a warm-up, then generalizes the technique to delimited control, and combines it with Filinski’s monadic reflection to support arbitrary monadic effects in direct style. It also discusses optimizations, performance benchmarks, and why the construction does not contradict prior impossibility results about expressing continuations with exceptions and state.

papers.title: Liquid Information Flow Control
papers.abstract: We present Lifty, a domain-specific language for data-centric applications that statically enforces declarative security policies using liquid types. Programmers annotate sensitive data sources with policies, and Lifty checks information flow automatically without manual proofs or annotations. When verification fails, Lifty localizes leaks and synthesizes provably correct repair patches, typically by guarding accesses with policy checks and redacting sensitive values on failure. The paper describes the TIO security monad, its liquid-type-based static IFC encoding, an operational and formal type system, and an implementation evaluated on microbenchmarks and case studies such as conference management, health portals, and grade records.

papers.title: Synthesizing Entity Matching Rules by Examples
papers.abstract: We study how to synthesize entity matching rules from positive and negative examples. The paper defines General Boolean Formula (GBF) rules for entity matching, which can combine attribute-matching predicates with conjunction, disjunction, negation, and conditional if-then-else structure. It formulates the task as a syntax-guided synthesis problem and proposes RuleSynth, an algorithm that combines CEGIS, RANSAC-style sampling, and a custom threshold solver to search the rule space efficiently. The method aims to produce concise, interpretable rules while maintaining strong matching accuracy. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show that the synthesized rules outperform other interpretable models and are competitive with several non-interpretable machine learning methods.

papers.title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
papers.abstract: Federal Information Processing Standards Publication 197 announces the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) and specifies the Rijndael block cipher as a FIPS-approved symmetric encryption algorithm. It defines the standard’s scope, applicability, implementation requirements, and key sizes (128, 192, and 256 bits) for 128-bit blocks. The specification describes the internal state representation, finite-field arithmetic, and the round transformations SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey, along with key expansion, inverse cipher operations, and implementation guidance. Appendices provide key expansion examples, a cipher example, example vectors, and references.

papers.title: RVISmith: Fuzzing Compilers for RVV Intrinsics
papers.abstract: RVISmith is a randomized fuzzer for compilers handling RVV (RISC-V Vector Extension) intrinsics. It generates well-defined C programs with varied RVV intrinsic invocation sequences, aiming for high intrinsic coverage, richer sequence variety, and avoidance of known undefined behaviors. The paper describes sequence selection, vector-register allocation, intrinsic scheduling, and code generation, along with a differential testing framework across compilers, optimizations, and equivalent programs. Evaluations on GCC, LLVM, and XuanTie show 11.5× higher intrinsic coverage than the prior RVV fuzzer RIF and reveal 13 previously unknown bugs, 10 confirmed and 3 fixed by developers.

The work standardizes CAD reconstruction as recovering a program from target geometry and benchmarks neurally guided search methods using face-adjacency graph representations and imitation-learned policies. papers.title: Beyond Rules: LLM-Powered Linting for Quantum Programs
papers.abstract: The paper presents LintQ-LLM+CoT and LintQ-LLM+RAG, LLM-based approaches for detecting quantum programming problems in Qiskit code. They extend a prior LLM linter with multi-prompt chain-of-thought reasoning and, for RAG, retrieval from a curated knowledge base of verified problem examples. In a manual evaluation over 55 Qiskit programs, both approaches outperform the rule-based baseline LintQ on precision, recall, and F1-score. LintQ-LLM+CoT achieves the best overall effectiveness and recall, while LintQ-LLM+RAG attains slightly higher precision by reducing false positives. The study argues that LLMs can provide a more adaptable foundation for quantum software linting than rigid rule-based static analysis.

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs, the Missing Link in Agentic AI-based Formal Verification
papers.abstract: Recent LLM-based workflows can generate SystemVerilog Assertions from natural-language specifications, but ambiguity, missing RTL context, and syntax failures limit quality. This paper proposes a verification-centric knowledge graph built from typed intermediate representations of the specification, RTL, and formal-tool feedback. Multi-agent workflows query and update the graph to generate assertions and perform syntax repair, counterexample-guided correction, and coverage-directed augmentation. Evaluated on seven benchmark designs, the approach improves specification-to-RTL grounding and produces compilable assertions with low repair overhead, achieving formal coverage from 78.5% to 99.4%.

papers.title: Synthesizing theories of human language with Bayesian program induction
papers.abstract: We present a Bayesian program induction framework for synthesizing interpretable theories of morpho-phonology from sparse form-meaning data. The system infers language-specific lexica and ordered phonological rules, using program synthesis and SAT-based search to scale across 70 textbook datasets from 58 languages. It recovers substantial portions of gold lexica and rules, learns cross-language metatheoretic biases via fragment grammars, and improves difficult cases through hierarchical Bayesian inference. The same approach also captures few-shot artificial grammar learning phenomena, linking language acquisition and linguistic theory discovery.

papers.title: Improved modeling of RNA-binding protein motifs in an interpretable neural model of RNA splicing
papers.abstract: The paper presents Sparse Adjusted Motif (SAM), a modular neural architecture for gene-level RNA splicing prediction that combines a local splice site identifier, sparse RNA-binding protein motif models, and an aggregator. Using in vitro RNA binding models for 79 human RBPs and genome sequence, the authors compare fixed motifs, adjusted motifs, and neural baselines. Adjusted motifs are trained end-to-end for splicing while remaining anchored to known RBPs, improving splice-site prediction and better matching independent eCLIP, MPRA, and RBP knockdown data. The work emphasizes enforced sparsity and modularity to preserve interpretability and enable motif-level analyses and variant interpretation.

papers.title: Sparling: end-to-end spatial concept learning via extremely sparse activations
papers.abstract: The paper studies when sparse, local latent intermediate variables (“motifs”) can be recovered from end-to-end supervision alone. It proves a Motif Identifiability Theorem: under non-overlapping motifs, motif sufficiency, and α-motif-necessity, low end-to-end error implies low motif error. To make such recovery practical, it introduces SPARLING, which uses a spatial sparsity layer with adaptive quantile thresholds and annealed target density to enforce extreme activation sparsity. Experiments on synthetic digit, OCR, and audio sequence domains show that very sparse intermediate layers can recover motifs with high accuracy, while a splicing domain that violates assumptions performs worse but still above chance.

papers.title: ENCOMPASS: Enhancing Agent Programming with Search Over Program Execution Paths
papers.abstract: We present ENCOMPASS, a Python framework for agent programming that separates agent workflow logic from inference-time search strategy via probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN). Programmers mark unreliable operations, such as LLM calls, with branchpoints; the framework compiles the program into a search space over execution paths. ENCOMPASS supports common strategies including best-of-N sampling, beam search, refinement, backtracking with memory, self-consistency, and custom search algorithms. Case studies on code repository translation, ARC-style hypothesis search, and Reflexion-style agents show that ENCOMPASS makes it easier to experiment with search strategies and can improve reliability and scaling while requiring little additional code.
